title: No. 69 — The Real Character of the Executive (Hamilton)
paragraphs: I now proceed to trace the real character of the proposed Executive as the Convention's plan marks it out. This will show in a strong light how unfair the representations made about it have been.

The first thing that strikes us is that the executive authority, with few exceptions, is to be placed in a single chief executive. Yet this can hardly be treated as a basis for comparison. If in this respect there is a resemblance to the king of Great Britain, there is just as much resemblance to the Grand Seignior, to the khan of Tartary, to the Man of the Seven Mountains, or to the governor of New York.

This chief executive is to be elected for four years, and he may be re-elected as often as the people of the United States think him worthy of their confidence. In these respects he is wholly unlike a king of Great Britain, who is a hereditary monarch and holds the crown as a family property that passes to his heirs forever. But he is closely like a governor of New York, who is elected for three years and may be re-elected without limit or interruption. Consider how much less time it would take to build up a dangerous influence in a single State than to build up the same influence across the United States. We must conclude that a four-year term for the chief executive of the Union is a degree of permanence far less to be feared in that office than a three-year term for the corresponding office in a single State.

The President of the United States could be impeached and tried. If convicted of treason, bribery or other high crimes or misdemeanors, he would be removed from office, and afterward he could still be prosecuted and punished in the ordinary course of law. The person of the king of Great Britain is sacred and inviolable. There is no constitutional court to which he answers, and no punishment can be inflicted on him without bringing on the crisis of a national revolution. On this delicate and important matter of personal responsibility, the President of Confederated America would stand on no better ground than a governor of New York, and on worse ground than the governors of Maryland and Delaware.

The President is to have the power to send back for reconsideration a bill that has passed both branches of the legislature, and the bill so returned becomes law if, on reconsideration, two thirds of both houses approve it. The king of Great Britain, for his part, holds an absolute negative on the acts of the two houses of Parliament. That this power has not been used for a considerable time does not change the fact that it exists. The reason is wholly that the crown has found a way to substitute influence for authority, that is, the art of winning a majority in one or the other house, in place of exercising a prerogative that could seldom be used without risking some degree of national disturbance. The President's qualified negative differs widely from the British sovereign's absolute one, and matches exactly the power of revision held by the council of revision of this State, of which the governor is one member. In this respect the President's power would exceed that of the governor of New York, because the President would hold alone what the governor shares with the chancellor and judges. But it would be precisely the same as that of the governor of Massachusetts, whose constitution, on this point, seems to have been the model the Convention copied.

The President is to be the "commander-in-chief of the army and navy of the United States, and of the militia of the several States, when called into the actual service of the United States. He is to have power to grant reprieves and pardons for offenses against the United States, except in cases of impeachment; to recommend to the consideration of Congress such measures as he shall judge necessary and expedient; to convene, on extraordinary occasions, both houses of the legislature, or either of them, and, in case of disagreement between them with respect to the time of adjournment, to adjourn them to such time as he shall think proper; to take care that the laws be faithfully executed; and to commission all officers of the United States." In most of these respects the President's power will resemble equally that of the king of Great Britain and that of the governor of New York. The most important points of difference are these. First. The President will have only occasional command of that part of the nation's militia which legislative provision may call into the actual service of the Union. The king of Great Britain and the governor of New York have at all times full command of all the militia within their separate jurisdictions. On this point, therefore, the President's power would be inferior to that of either the monarch or the governor. Second. The President is to be commander-in-chief of the army and navy of the United States. In this respect his authority would be the same as the British king's in name, but much less in substance. It would amount to no more than the supreme command and direction of the military and naval forces, as first General and admiral of the Confederacy. The British king's authority extends to declaring war and to raising and regulating fleets and armies, all of which, under the Constitution now before us, would belong to the legislature.(1) The governor of New York, on the other hand, is given by the State constitution only the command of its militia and navy. But the constitutions of several of the States expressly declare their governors commanders-in-chief of the army as well as the navy, and it may well be a question whether those of New Hampshire and Massachusetts in particular do not give their governors larger powers on this point than a President of the United States could claim. Third. The President's power over pardons would extend to all cases except impeachment. The governor of New York may pardon in all cases, even impeachment, except treason and murder. Is not the governor's power on this point, reckoned by its political consequences, greater than the President's? All conspiracies and plots against the government that have not ripened into actual treason may be shielded from any punishment by the interposition of the pardoning prerogative. If a governor of New York, then, were at the head of such a conspiracy, he could guarantee his accomplices and followers complete impunity until the design had ripened into actual hostility. A President of the Union, on the other hand, though he may even pardon treason when it is prosecuted in the ordinary course of law, could not shelter any offender, in any degree, from the effects of impeachment and conviction. Would not the prospect of total immunity for all the preliminary steps be a greater temptation to start and persist in an enterprise against public liberty than the mere prospect of escaping death and confiscation if the final execution of the design should fail in an actual appeal to arms? Would this last expectation have any influence at all, once one calculated the probability that the person who was to grant the exemption might himself be caught up in the consequences of the scheme, and might be made unable, by his own part in it, to give the impunity desired? To judge this matter better, we must recall that under the proposed Constitution the offense of treason is limited "to levying war upon the United States, and adhering to their enemies, giving them aid and comfort," and that under the laws of New York it is confined within similar bounds. Fourth. The President can adjourn the national legislature only in the single case of disagreement about the time of adjournment. The British monarch may prorogue Parliament or even dissolve it. The governor of New York may also prorogue the legislature of this State for a limited time, a power that in certain situations may be used for very important purposes.

The President is to have the power, with the advice and consent of the Senate, to make treaties, provided two thirds of the senators present concur. The king of Great Britain is the sole and absolute representative of the nation in all foreign dealings. He can make treaties of peace, commerce, alliance and every other kind entirely on his own. It has been hinted that his authority here is not final, and that his agreements with foreign powers are subject to the review of Parliament and need its ratification. But I believe this doctrine was never heard of until it was brought up on the present occasion. Every jurist(2) of that kingdom, and every other man acquainted with its Constitution, knows as an established fact that the prerogative of making treaties exists in the crown in its fullest extent, and that compacts made by royal authority have complete legal validity and perfection, independent of any other sanction. Parliament, it is true, is sometimes seen altering existing laws to bring them into line with the terms of a new treaty, and this may have given rise to the idea that its cooperation was necessary to make the treaty binding. But this parliamentary intervention has a different cause. It comes from the need to fit a highly artificial and intricate system of revenue and commercial laws to the changes the treaty makes in them, and to adapt new provisions and precautions to the new state of things, so as to keep the machine from running into disorder. In this respect, then, there is no comparison between the intended power of the President and the actual power of the British sovereign. The one can do alone what the other can do only with the concurrence of a branch of the legislature. It must be admitted that in this instance the power of the federal Executive would exceed that of any State Executive. But this follows naturally from the sovereign power that relates to treaties. If the Confederacy were dissolved, it would become a question whether the Executives of the individual States would not alone be invested with that delicate and important prerogative.

The President is also to be authorized to receive ambassadors and other public ministers. This has been a rich theme of declamation, but it is more a matter of dignity than of authority. It will have no consequence in the administration of the government, and it was far more convenient to arrange things this way than to make it necessary to convene the legislature, or one of its branches, at every arrival of a foreign minister, even if only to fill the place of a predecessor who had left.

The President is to nominate and, with the advice and consent of the Senate, to appoint ambassadors and other public ministers, judges of the Supreme Court, and in general all officers of the United States who are established by law and whose appointments the Constitution does not otherwise provide for. The king of Great Britain is emphatically and truly called the fountain of honor. He not only appoints to all offices but can create offices. He can confer titles of nobility at will, and he has the disposal of an immense number of church positions. The President's power in this respect is plainly far inferior to the British king's. Nor is it equal to that of the governor of New York, if we judge the meaning of the State's constitution by the practice that has grown up under it. The power of appointment among us is lodged in a council made up of the governor and four members of the Senate, chosen by the Assembly. The governor claims, and has often exercised, the right of nomination, and he is entitled to a casting vote in the appointment. If he really has the right of nominating, his authority here equals the President's and exceeds it in the matter of the casting vote. In the national government, if the Senate should be divided, no appointment could be made. In the government of New York, if the council should be divided, the governor can turn the scale and confirm his own nomination.(3) Compare the publicity that must necessarily attend the President's appointments, made with an entire branch of the national legislature, to the privacy of the governor of New York's, who sits closeted in a secret room with at most four people, and often with only two. At the same time, consider how much easier it must be to influence the small number that a council of appointment consists of than the considerable number that the national Senate would consist of. We cannot hesitate to conclude that the power of this State's chief executive in handing out offices must, in practice, be greatly superior to that of the chief executive of the Union.

It appears from all this that, apart from the President's shared authority in the matter of treaties, it would be hard to say whether that official would, taken as a whole, hold more or less power than the Governor of New York. And it appears still more clearly that the parallel attempted between him and the king of Great Britain has no basis at all. But to make the contrast in this respect still more striking, it may be useful to bring the principal points of difference together in a closer group.

The President of the United States would be an officer elected by the people for four years; the king of Great Britain is a perpetual and hereditary prince. The one would be liable to personal punishment and disgrace; the person of the other is sacred and inviolable. The one would have a qualified negative on the acts of the legislative body; the other has an absolute negative. The one would have the right to command the military and naval forces of the nation; the other has this right and in addition holds that of declaring war and of raising and regulating fleets and armies by his own authority. The one would share with a branch of the legislature the power of making treaties; the other is the sole holder of that power. The one would share in the same way in appointing to offices; the other is the sole source of all appointments. The one can grant no privileges whatever; the other can make denizens of aliens (foreigners granted residence and some of the rights of citizens) and noblemen of commoners, and can create corporations with all the rights that belong to corporate bodies. The one can set no rules about the nation's commerce or currency; the other is in several respects the arbiter of commerce, and in that capacity can establish markets and fairs, regulate weights and measures, lay embargoes for a limited time, coin money, and authorize or prohibit the circulation of foreign coin. The one has not a particle of spiritual jurisdiction; the other is the supreme head and governor of the national church! What answer shall we give to those who would persuade us that things so unlike resemble each other? The same answer that ought to be given to those who tell us that a government whose entire power would be in the hands of the elected servants of the people, who are chosen at regular intervals, is an aristocracy, a monarchy and a despotism.

1. A writer in a Pennsylvania paper, under the signature of TAMONY, has asserted that the king of Great Britain owes his prerogative as commander-in-chief to an annual mutiny bill. The truth is, on the contrary, that his prerogative in this respect is immemorial, and was disputed only, "contrary to all reason and precedent," as Blackstone vol. i., page 262, puts it, by the Long Parliament of Charles I. But by the statute of the 13th of Charles II., chap. 6, it was declared to be in the king alone, because the sole supreme government and command of the militia within his Majesty's realms and dominions, and of all forces by sea and land, and of all forts and places of strength, EVER WAS AND IS the undoubted right of his Majesty and his royal predecessors, kings and queens of England, and both or either house of Parliament cannot nor ought to pretend to the same.
2. Vide Blackstone's Commentaries, Vol I., p. 257.

3. Honesty requires me to admit, however, that I do not think the governor's claim to a right of nomination is well founded. Still, it is always fair to reason from how a government actually operates, until that practice has been challenged on constitutional grounds. And even setting this claim aside, if we weigh the other considerations and follow them out to all their consequences, we shall be inclined to reach much the same conclusion.
